# Evaluating the Limit with the Dirac Delta

## Setting Up the Problem

We need to evaluate:
$$\lim_{h\to0}\int_{-h}^h \delta(i+x)\,f(x)\,dx$$

The Dirac delta $\delta(i+x) = \delta(x - (-i))$ is centered at $x = -i$.

## Applying the Sifting Property

The sifting property of the Dirac delta states:
$$\int_a^b \delta(x - c)\,f(x)\,dx = \begin{cases} f(c) & \text{if } c \in (a,b) \\ 0 & \text{if } c \notin [a,b] \end{cases}$$

Here, the "center" of the delta is at $c = -i$, and the integration interval is $[-h,\, h]$.

## Analyzing the Limit

As $h \to 0^+$, the interval $[-h, h]$ shrinks to the single point $\{0\}$.

Since the delta is centered at $x = -i$ (with $i \neq 0$), there exists $\varepsilon = |i| > 0$ such that for all $0 < h < |i|$:
$$x = -i \notin [-h, h]$$

Therefore, for all sufficiently small $h$, the point where the delta is concentrated lies **outside** the integration interval, and:
$$\int_{-h}^h \delta(i+x)\,f(x)\,dx = 0$$

## Conclusion

Since the integrand (in the distributional sense) contributes nothing within $[-h,h]$ for all small enough $h$, the limit is:

$$\lim_{h\to0}\int_{-h}^h \delta(i+x)\,f(x)\,dx = 0$$

$$\boxed{0}$$

27B·v4.method: Identifies the delta's center at x=−i, applies the sifting property to show the integral vanishes when the center lies outside the shrinking interval [−h,h], concluding the limit is 0 for non-zero i.
